sec.title: Background
sec.p: This study evaluated the efficacy and safety of mecapegfilgrastim for preventing immunochemotherapy‐induced neutropenia in treatment‐naive patients with diffuse large B‐cell lymphoma (DLBCL).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In this open‐label, multicenter exploratory trial, patients were randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive mecapegfilgrastim or no prophylaxis. All participants received 4 cycles of R‐CHOP or R‐CHOP‐like regimens. The primary endpoint was the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia during cycle 1.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Between October 2021 and June 2024, 42 patients were enrolled (mecapegfilgrastim: n = 28; control: n = 14). Grade ≥ 3 neutropenia in cycle 1 occurred in 32.14% of the mecapegfilgrastim group versus 64.29% in the control group. Across all cycles, mecapegfilgrastim consistently reduced grade ≥ 3 neutropenia; nadir neutrophil counts were higher and the need for short‐acting granulocyte colony‐stimulating factor was lower in the mecapegfilgrastim group (all nominal p ≤ 0.05). No cases of febrile neutropenia occurred in the mecapegfilgrastim group, compared to one case in the control group. Objective response rates were 75.0% (95% CI: 55.1, 89.3) and 57.1% (95% CI: 28.9, 82.3), respectively (nominal p = 0.298). Mecapegfilgrastim reduced the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia regardless of treatment response. Grade ≥ 3 treatment‐emergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 42.9% of the mecapegfilgrastim group and 92.9% of controls; serious TEAEs were reported in 7.1% of patients in both groups.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Mecapegfilgrastim demonstrated a favorable safety profile and potential efficacy in reducing the incidence and severity of neutropenia in DLBCL patients receiving R‐CHOP or R‐CHOP‐like regimens. These findings may support its prophylactic use in this population and warrant validation in larger trials.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Diffuse large B‐cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most prevalent subtype of non‐Hodgkin lymphoma, accounting for approximately one‐third of all cases [1]. The current first‐line standard treatment for DLBCL is the rituximab with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R‐CHOP) regimen. Neutropenia is a common and severe adverse event (AE) associated with R‐CHOP treatment, often resulting in treatment delays, dose reductions, or discontinuation. These disruptions can further elevate the risk of febrile neutropenia (FN) and serious infections, which not only compromise treatment efficacy but also increase healthcare costs and pose potentially life‐threatening complications [2, 3].

Granulocyte colony‐stimulating factor (G‐CSF) is widely used to prevent chemotherapy‐induced neutropenia (CIN) and FN. Studies have demonstrated that prophylactic administration of G‐CSF can reduce the duration of CIN in patients with malignant lymphoma and solid tumors, lower the incidence of FN and infections, and increase the relative dose intensity. These benefits, in turn, minimize the need for antibiotics and hospitalizations, while also reducing early mortality rates, particularly those associated with infections [4, 5, 6].

There are two types of G‐CSF: short‐acting and long‐acting. Short‐acting G‐CSF effectively stimulates the production and maturation of neutrophils, thus preventing CIN and FN; however, its relatively short half‐life necessitates daily injections. Long‐acting G‐CSF, developed by conjugating polyethylene glycol (PEG) of a specified molecular weight to the N‐terminal amino acid of short‐acting G‐CSF (filgrastim), retains the core protein while increasing molecular weight. This modification reduces the glomerular filtration rate and prolongs the drug's circulation half‐life. Additionally, pegylated recombinant human G‐CSF (PEG‐rhG‐CSF) inhibits proteolytic hydrolysis, decreasing the rate of protein degradation. Its clearance is primarily mediated by neutrophils and their progenitor cells rather than by renal filtration. This mechanism allows PEG‐rhG‐CSF's clearance to be self‐regulating, occurring only once neutrophil recovery begins [7]. Studies have shown that PEG‐rhG‐CSF achieves efficacy at least comparable to that of short‐acting G‐CSF, with no significant differences in toxicity. However, PEG‐rhG‐CSF has the advantage of a longer half‐life and extended duration of action, requiring only a single injection per chemotherapy cycle [8, 9]. This enhances convenience for clinical application. Moreover, real‐world studies involving breast cancer patients suggest that PEG‐rhG‐CSF may be more cost‐effective than short‐acting G‐CSF for CIN prevention [10, 11].

However, data on the efficacy and safety of long‐acting recombinant human G‐CSF (rhG‐CSF) for preventing neutropenia in DLBCL patients undergoing R‐CHOP treatment are limited, particularly regarding prospective studies [3, 12]. Mecapegfilgrastim is a long‐acting PEG‐rhG‐CSF and a biosimilar of pegfilgrastim. Its efficacy and safety in preventing CIN and FN have been established across several cancer types, including breast cancer and non‐small cell lung cancer [13, 14]. However, no studies to date have specifically evaluated the efficacy and safety of mecapegfilgrastim in preventing immunochemotherapy‐induced neutropenia in patients with DLBCL [15, 16].

Based on this background, the present study aimed to investigate the prophylactic efficacy of mecapegfilgrastim in preventing immunochemotherapy‐induced neutropenia in treatment‐naive DLBCL patients receiving R‐CHOP or R‐CHOP‐like regimens.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: This study was an open‐label, multicenter, randomized, controlled exploratory trial (NO. ChiCTR2100048196), conducted from October 2021 to June 2024 at four sites across China: West China Hospital, Sichuan University (n = 28), Nanchong Central Hospital (n = 6), Deyang People's Hospital (n = 5), and the Affiliated Hospital of North Sichuan Medical College (n = 3). The trial adheres to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki and complies with Good Clinical Practice guidelines. The study protocol and its amendments received approval from the Ethics Committee on Biomedical Research, West China Hospital of Sichuan University (Approval No. 2021–576). Informed consent was obtained from each participant prior to the initiation of treatment.

sec.title: Study Population
sec.p: The primary inclusion criteria for this study were patients aged 18–75 years who were scheduled to receive standard R‐CHOP or R‐CHOP‐like regimens, with a histopathological diagnosis of CD20‐positive, unspecified DLBCL. Eligible patients had no prior systemic immunochemotherapy for CD20‐positive DLBCL, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 to 3, an expected survival time of at least 4 months, and an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of ≥ 2.0 × 109/L prior to immunochemotherapy. Key exclusion criteria included pregnant or breastfeeding women, patients with transformed DLBCL, a history of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation or previous immunochemotherapy/radiotherapy for malignancies, active infection requiring systemic antibiotics within 72 h before immunochemotherapy, and severe dysfunction of the liver, kidneys, heart, or lungs. An additional movie file shows this in more detail (Table S1).

sec.title: Treatments
sec.p: Eligible subjects were randomly assigned to either the mecapegfilgrastim or control group in a 2:1 ratio, with randomization codes generated using a random number table through the Interactive Web Response System. Patients in both groups were scheduled to receive standard R‐CHOP or R‐CHOP‐like regimens, with each treatment cycle lasting 21 days. Participants were monitored for a total of 4 cycles. The initial dosing for the standard R‐CHOP regimen was as follows: rituximab, 375 mg/m2 by intravenous infusion on day 1; cyclophosphamide, 750 mg/m2 by intravenous infusion on day 2; doxorubicin, 50 mg/m2 by intravenous infusion on day 2; vincristine, 1.4 mg/m2 by intravenous infusion on day 2; and prednisone, 100 mg orally from days 2–6. The specific dosing for the R‐CHOP‐like regimen was adjusted by the study physicians according to each patient individual condition. At 24–48 h after each R‐CHOP cycle, patients in the mecapegfilgrastim group received a single subcutaneous injection of a fixed dose of 6 mg mecapegfilgrastim. In contrast, patients in the control group received no preventive intervention and were solely observed. If a patient's ANC was ≤ 0.5 × 109/L in the mecapegfilgrastim group or < 1.0 × 109/L in the control group, short‐acting rhG‐CSF (5 μg/kg/day, subcutaneously) was permitted as rescue therapy until the ANC recovered to ≥ 5.0 × 109/L. In the mecapegfilgrastim group, blood samples for routine blood examination were collected on days 1, 5, 7, 9, 13, and 17 (±1) of cycle 1, and on days 1, 5, 9, and 13 (±1) for cycles 2 through 4. In the control group, routine blood tests were performed on days 1, 5, 9, and 13 (±1) of each cycle from 1 to 4.

sec.title: Study Endpoints
sec.p: The primary endpoint was the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia (ANC < 1.0 × 109/L) in each group during the first immunochemotherapy cycle. The secondary endpoints include the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia and FN during cycles 1–4, the proportion of patients experiencing immunochemotherapy delays in subsequent cycles due to ANC < 0.5 × 109/L, the proportion of patients with dose reductions in cycles 2–4 due to ANC < 0.5 × 109/L, the incidence of infections and antibiotic usage due to ANC < 0.5 × 109/L during cycles 1–4, and safety. Additionally, this study also analyzed the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia, the incidence of grade 4 neutropenia, the mean nadir ANC value across each immunochemotherapy cycle, the use of short‐acting G‐CSF, the objective response rate (ORR), and the incidence of grade ≥ 3 and grade 4 neutropenia in both patients who achieved ORR and those who did not during cycles 1–4. FN was defined as an oral temperature exceeding 38.3°C (axillary temperature > 38.1°C) or two consecutive oral temperature readings > 38.0°C (axillary temperature > 37.8°C) within 2 h, accompanied by an ANC < 0.5 × 109/L or predicted to fall below that threshold. AEs were recorded and graded according to the National Cancer Institute's Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0, encompassing AEs occurring during treatment and within 30 days following the last administration.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: The analysis for the efficacy endpoints in this study was based on the full analysis set, which included all enrolled patients who received at least one dose of mecapegfilgrastim in the mecapegfilgrastim group or completed at least 1 cycle of R‐CHOP/R‐CHOP‐like regimen in the control group. For safety evaluations, the safety analysis set also comprised all enrolled patients who received at least one dose of mecapegfilgrastim in the mecapegfilgrastim group or completed at least 1 cycle of R‐CHOP/R‐CHOP‐like regimen in the control group. Categorical data were reported as the number of patients (n) and corresponding percentages (%). For the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia (ANC < 1.0 × 109/L) during the first cycle of immunochemotherapy, the 95% confidence interval (CI) for the rates was calculated using the Clopper‐Pearson method, and inter‐group comparisons were performed with the chi‐square test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. The 95% CI for the difference in rates between groups was determined using the Miettinen–Nurminen method. For continuous data, the number of non‐missing patients (n), arithmetic mean, standard deviation, median, minimum, and maximum were reported. Inter‐group comparisons for continuous variables were conducted using either the t‐tests or the Wilcoxon rank–sum test. For longitudinal ANC measurements during cycle 1, a mixed‐effects model for repeated measures was used to assess temporal trends between groups. Subgroup analysis of the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia during cycle 1 was conducted across different populations (age, bone marrow involvement, liver function, renal function, and ECOG score) to assess the impact of baseline characteristics on the efficacy of mecapegfilgrastim. Subgroup analyses were exploratory and not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Nominal p values are reported without adjustment for multiple testing. Overall survival (OS) was estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with corresponding 95% CIs calculated using the Greenwood formula. Differences between groups were evaluated using the log‐rank test, and hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs were estimated using the Cox proportional hazards model. All statistical analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4.

sec.title: Baseline Characteristics
sec.p: From October 2021 to June 2024, a total of 42 patients were enrolled (Figure 1). The baseline characteristics of the patients are summarized in Table 1. In the mecapegfilgrastim group, 28 patients were included, with a median age of 58 years (range: 33–75 years), and 13 patients (46.4%) were male. In the control group, 14 patients were included, with a median age of 46 years (range: 26–74 years), and six patients (42.9%) were male. The baseline ANC in the mecapegfilgrastim group was 4.20 ± 2.8 × 109/L, compared to 4.39 ± 2.3 × 109/L in the control group. Overall, baseline characteristics were generally balanced between groups. White blood cell counts and platelet counts were similar, whereas hemoglobin levels were slightly higher in the mecapegfilgrastim group compared with the control group.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: In the first cycle of immunochemotherapy, 32.14% (9/28, [95% CI: 15.88, 52.35]) of patients in the mecapegfilgrastim group and 64.29% (9/14, [95% CI: 35.14, 87.24]) in the control group experienced grade ≥ 3 neutropenia, resulting in a numerical difference of −32.14% (95% CI: −58.23, −0.01; nominal p = 0.096). In subsequent immunochemotherapy cycles (2, 3 and 4), as well as across all cycles (1–4), the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia was lower in the mecapegfilgrastim group compared to the control group, with nominal p‐values for cycles 3, 4, and 1–4 all being ≤ 0.05. Additionally, the mecapegfilgrastim group had a lower incidence of grade 4 neutropenia compared to the control group, with numerical differences observed across individual cycles (cycles 1, 2, 3, and 4) and the overall study period (cycles 1–4) as follows: −32.14% (95% CI, −58.82, −0.98), −6.69% (95% CI, −35.42, 15.37), −13.18% (95% CI, −44.14, 9.89), −9.09% (95% CI, −38.33, 10.07), and −28.57% (95% CI, −55.77, 2.83), respectively (all nominal p‐values > 0.05). The mecapegfilgrastim group also showed higher mean nadir ANC values (all nominal p‐values ≤ 0.05). No patients in the mecapegfilgrastim group experienced FN, whereas one patient in the control group developed FN (7.14%; 95% CI: 0.18, 33.87) (Table 2).

sec.p: The profile of mean ANC during cycle 1 in the mecapegfilgrastim group demonstrated a rapid increase following administration, peaking on day 5, and then gradually declining. After reaching its nadir on day 9, the mean ANC began to rebound, achieving a second peak on day 13, followed by a slow decline thereafter (Figure 2). In contrast, the mean ANC curve for the control group remained relatively flat, consistently staying at a lower level throughout the observation period (Figure 2). The difference in ANC trends between the two groups was statistically significant (mixed‐effects model, p = 0.0167).

sec.p: The usage rates of short‐acting G‐CSF across cycles 1, 2, 3, and 4, as well as for the overall cycles 1–4, were markedly lower in the mecapegfilgrastim group compared to the control groups. The usage rates were 3.57% versus 57.14% in cycle 1, 0% versus 30.77% in cycle 2, 0% versus 18.18% in cycle 3, 0% versus 36.36% in cycle 4, and 3.57% versus 64.29% for overall cycles 1–4. The corresponding rate differences were −53.57% (95% CI, −76.10, −26.75), −30.77% (95% CI, −57.98, −12.52), −18.18% (95% CI, −48.20, 0.32), −36.36% (95% CI, −65.04, −14.42), and −60.71% (95% CI, −81.20, −33.09), respectively. Nominal p‐values were ≤ 0.05 for all cycles, except cycle 3 (Table 3). During immunochemotherapy cycles 1–2, 2–3, and 3–4, the mecapegfilgrastim group had 4.35% (1/23), 5.00% (1/20), and 0% of patients experiencing immunochemotherapy delays due to ANC < 0.5 × 109/L, which was lower than the control group (15.38% [2/13], 9.09% [1/11], and 9.09% [1/11], respectively), with nominal p‐values all > 0.05 (Table 4). Additionally, for the evaluable cycles 1–2 and 2–3, the duration of immunochemotherapy delays was also shorter in the mecapegfilgrastim group. Both groups had no patients with dose reductions due to ANC < 0.5 × 109/L. The mecapegfilgrastim group had one case (3.57%) of infection requiring antibiotic use due to ANC < 0.5 × 109/L, compared to two cases (14.29%) in the control group (nominal p = 0.2537).

sec.p: In the mecapegfilgrastim group, 75% (95% Exact CI, 55.1–89.3) of patients achieved ORR, with 57.1% (16/28) achieving complete response (CR) and 17.9% (5/28) achieving partial response (PR). In the control group, 57% (95% Exact CI, 28.9–82.3) achieved ORR, with 50.0% (7/14) achieving CR and 7.1% (1/14) achieving PR. There were no statistically significant differences between groups in ORR (p = 0.298), CR rate (p = 0.748), or PR rate (p = 0.645) (Table S2).

Regarding OS, median follow‐up time was 30.39 months (95% CI, 28.39, 36.60) in the mecapegfilgrastim group and 40.48 months (95% CI, 25.33, 46.82) in the control group. Median OS was not reached (NR; 95% CI, NR, NR) in the mecapegfilgrastim group and NR (95% CI, 15.47, NR) in the control group, with a HR of 0.49 (95% CI, 0.14, 1.69; p = 0.2469). The 12‐month OS rates were 92.86% in both groups; at 24 months, OS was 85.23% versus 71.43%; at 36 months, 80.74% versus 71.43%; and at 48 months, 80.74% versus 59.52% in the mecapegfilgrastim and control groups, respectively (Figure S1).

In both the subgroups with ORR achieved and not achieved, the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia during immunochemotherapy cycles 1–4 was lower in the mecapegfilgrastim group compared to the control group (for ORR achieved: 38.1% vs 87.5%, nominal p = 0.0352; for ORR not achieved: 28.6% vs 100.0%, nominal p = 0.0210). Similarly, the incidence of grade 4 neutropenia was lower as well (for ORR achieved: 28.6% vs 62.5%, nominal p = 0.1975; for ORR not achieved: 28.6% vs 50.0%, nominal p = 0.5921) (Table S3).

To determine whether baseline characteristics influence the evaluation of the primary endpoint, this study conducted a subgroup analysis of neutropenia incidence in cycle 1 based on age (≤ 65 years and > 65 years), bone marrow involvement (present and absent), liver function (bilirubin: ≤ 2 mg/dL and > 2 mg/dL), renal function (creatinine clearance rate: < 50 mL/min and ≥ 50 mL/min), and ECOG score (0 and 1). The results indicated that although the odds ratios (OR) values in all subgroups suggested a potential benefit of mecapegfilgrastim, statistical significance was only achieved in patients aged ≤ 65 years (OR, 0.14; 95% CI, 0.02, 0.88), though this should be interpreted cautiously given the small subgroup sample. Notably, in the overall population, the OR value was 0.26 (95% CI: 0.07, 1.02). (Table S4).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: In the mecapegfilgrastim group, 60.7% (17/28) of patients experienced any grade treatment‐emergent AEs (TEAEs), whereas the control group had a TEAE incidence of 100.0% (14/14) (Table 5). Grade ≥ 3 TEAEs occurred in 42.9% (12/28) of patients in the mecapegfilgrastim group and 92.9% (13/14) in the control group. These TEAEs included decreased ANC (10 cases [35.7%] in the mecapegfilgrastim group vs 13 cases [92.9%] in the control group), decreased white blood cell count (nine cases [32.1%] vs eight cases [57.1%]), infectious pneumonia (two cases [7.1%] vs one case [7.1%]), and interstitial lung disease (one case [3.6%] vs 0 cases). The incidence of serious TEAEs was 7.1% in both groups, with two of 28 patients affected in the mecapegfilgrastim group and one of 14 patients in the control group. No patients in either the mecapegfilgrastim group or the control group experienced dose reductions, treatment suspension, or discontinuation due to TEAEs. One patient in the mecapegfilgrastim group succumbed to interstitial lung disease, which was deemed unrelated to mecapegfilgrastim.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This prospective, multicenter, randomized controlled trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of mecapegfilgrastim in preventing neutropenia among treatment‐naive patients with DLBCL undergoing standard R‐CHOP or R‐CHOP‐like regimens. To our knowledge, this is the first trial to specifically assess the prophylactic use of the long‐acting G‐CSF, mecapegfilgrastim, for the prevention of immunochemotherapy‐induced neutropenia in this patient population. The findings indicate that, in CD20‐positive, treatment‐naive DLBCL patients receiving R‐CHOP or R‐CHOP‐like regimens, mecapegfilgrastim demonstrated a favorable safety profile while effectively reducing the incidence of severe neutropenia, thereby limiting the requirement for rescue interventions.

Consistent with previous studies in lung cancer, long‐acting G‐CSF has demonstrated a substantial increase in ANC throughout chemotherapy [14, 17]. In this study, the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia in the first immunochemotherapy cycle decreased by 32.14% in the mecapegfilgrastim group compared to the control group (32.14% vs. 64.29%). Although statistical significance was not reached (nominal p = 0.0965), likely due to the limited sample size, the absolute risk reduction was substantial (32.14%), suggesting a promising clinically meaningful decrease in the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia. Subgroup analysis showed that in patients aged ≤ 65 years, the mecapegfilgrastim group significantly achieved a reduction in the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia during the first cycle. While the ORs in other subgroups also indicated a potential benefit of mecapegfilgrastim, the differences did not reach statistical significance, likely due to the small sample size and wide CIs. Notably, in the overall population, the OR was 0.26 (95% CI, 0.07, 1.02), suggesting a trend toward benefit. Additionally, the profile of mean ANC during cycle 1 showed that the mean ANC at various time points was consistently higher in the mecapegfilgrastim group compared to the control group. The pattern of ANC changes aligns with findings from previous studies [14]. In subsequent immunochemotherapy cycles (cycles 2, 3, and 4), as well as across the entire immunochemotherapy period (cycle 1–4), the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia was lower in the mecapegfilgrastim group compared to the control group. The differences between the two groups were −29.77%, −40.45%, −48.99%, and −57.14%, with nominal p‐values ≤ 0.05 for all cycles except cycle 2. As previous evaluations of long‐acting G‐CSF in DLBCL patients receiving R‐CHOP did not assess the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia, direct comparisons with the present study remain challenging [3, 12]. Nonetheless, the findings from this study offer preliminary evidence supporting the efficacy of mecapegfilgrastim in the prevention of immunochemotherapy‐induced neutropenia in DLBCL patients. These results align with efficacy data reported in previous studies involving patients with non‐small cell lung cancer and breast cancer [14, 18].

The incidence of grade 4 neutropenia was lower in the mecapegfilgrastim group compared to the control group across all immunochemotherapy cycles (with nominal p‐values > 0.05). Throughout the entire immunochemotherapy period, the mecapegfilgrastim group had a grade 4 neutropenia incidence of 28.57%, which was lower than the control group's 57.14% (nominal p = 0.0980). This proportion is similar to the findings reported in another study by Jeong et al. [3]. In that study, DLBCL patients receiving R‐CHOP treatment (up to 6–8 cycles) who were prophylactically treated with pegfilgrastim had a grade 4 neutropenia incidence of 29%, significantly lower than the 69.1% observed in the PROCESS cohort (p < 0.001) who did not receive prophylactic treatment. The key difference is that in our study, statistical significance was not reached, likely due to the smaller sample size.

In this study, no patients in the mecapegfilgrastim group experienced FN, while one patient (7.14%) in the control group developed FN. This result is consistent with the findings from phase III clinical trials of mecapegfilgrastim used prophylactically in patients with breast cancer [13] and non‐small cell lung cancer [14]. In contrast, a prospective cohort study conducted in Korea among DLBCL patients reported an FN incidence of 13.9% in those receiving the long‐acting G‐CSF pegfilgrastim for prevention [3]. Advanced age is a known risk factor for FN [3]. While retrospective studies have shown that long‐acting G‐CSFs like mecapegfilgrastim can reduce the incidence of FN, data suggest that in DLBCL patients aged 80 years and older, pegfilgrastim may be associated with a higher FN incidence [19, 20]. The median age of patients included in the Korean study (62 years [range: 19–86]) was six years higher than in our study (56 years [range: 26–76]), which may partly explain the differing FN incidences. Additionally, the subgroup analysis in this study indicated that patients aged ≤ 65 years had a lower risk of developing grade ≥ 3 neutropenia during the first cycle, suggesting that age may be an important influencing factor. Further research is warranted to evaluate the preventive efficacy of mecapegfilgrastim in elderly patients.

In this study, rescue treatment was administered when the ANC fell to ≤ 0.5 × 109/L in the mecapegfilgrastim group and < 1 × 109/L in the control group. The proportion of patients receiving rescue treatment was lower in the mecapegfilgrastim group compared to the control group across all immunochemotherapy cycles, with nominal p‐values ≤ 0.05 for all cycles except cycle 3. Throughout the entire treatment period, the rescue treatment rate in the mecapegfilgrastim group was 3.57%, compared to 64.29% in the control group (nominal p = 0.001). These findings suggest that mecapegfilgrastim may alleviate the severity of neutropenia, reduce the need for short‐acting G‐CSF injections, and enhance treatment convenience for patients with hematologic malignancies. This, in turn, has the potential to improve patients' overall quality of life. Additionally, the mean nadir ANC values during each immunochemotherapy cycle in the mecapegfilgrastim group were higher than those in the control group (with nominal p‐values ≤ 0.05), suggesting that mecapegfilgrastim may effectively reduce the severity of neutropenia in DLBCL patients. Similar trends have been observed in studies evaluating the efficacy and safety of other long‐acting G‐CSFs for CIN prevention in breast cancer patients [21, 22].

In comparing the tumor response between the mecapegfilgrastim group and the control group, the mecapegfilgrastim group demonstrated a higher ORR than the control group (75.0% vs 57.1%), although the difference was not statistically significant (nominal p = 0.298). This is consistent with previous studies, which have shown that G‐CSF agents do not directly affect tumor response [23, 24]. Instead, they help prevent immunochemotherapy‐induced neutropenia, reduce immunochemotherapy delays, maintain immunochemotherapy dose intensity, and thus improve treatment adherence, potentially enhancing long‐term patient outcomes [24, 25]. Consistent with this mechanism, although no statistically significant difference in OS was observed, the Kaplan–Meier curves suggested a separation favoring the mecapegfilgrastim group in the later follow‐up period. However, as this observation was based on exploratory analysis and was not supported by a statistically significant log‐rank test, it should be interpreted with caution. In addition, the limited sample size and relatively short follow‐up duration further restrict the ability to draw definitive conclusions regarding long‐term survival benefit. In this study, neither the mecapegfilgrastim group nor the control group had any patients with dose reductions due to ANC < 0.5 × 109/L. Furthermore, the proportion of patients in the mecapegfilgrastim group who experienced immunochemotherapy delays, the duration of those delays, infection rates, and antibiotic usage due to neutropenia were all lower than in the control group. Although no statistical significance was observed, this may be attributed to the small sample size. Additionally, the data showed that in both the ORR achieved and ORR not achieved subgroups, mecapegfilgrastim effectively reduced the incidence of grade ≥ 3 and grade 4 neutropenia, although the nominal p‐values for the latter were > 0.05, likely due to the sample size limitation. These results suggest that the efficacy of mecapegfilgrastim in preventing immunochemotherapy‐induced neutropenia in DLBCL patients is not affected by tumor response.

The safety data from this study show that mecapegfilgrastim is well tolerated, with a lower incidence of grade ≥ 3 TEAEs, while the incidence of serious TEAEs was comparable to that of the control group. No patients in either group required dose reductions, nor did any patients have their mecapegfilgrastim treatment interrupted or discontinued due to TEAEs. While one patient in the mecapegfilgrastim group died from interstitial lung disease, this event was considered unrelated to the drug. The most common AEs reported in the study (with an incidence of ≥ 10%) were decreased ANC, decreased white blood cell count, decreased hemoglobin, and lymphocytopenia. Previous studies have identified different common AEs, such as fatigue, bone pain, leukocytosis, and anemia [13, 14, 26], which may be attributed to variations in cancer types, immunochemotherapy regimens, or patient demographics.

This study has several limitations. First, the relatively small sample size may have limited the statistical power to detect differences between the mecapegfilgrastim and control groups, particularly for less frequent outcomes, and may also have resulted in incomplete balance of certain baseline characteristics despite randomization. Second, the follow‐up duration was relatively short, precluding a comprehensive assessment of long‐term survival benefits. Large‐scale studies with extended follow‐up are warranted to validate these findings further.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study is the first to demonstrate that the long‐acting G‐CSF, mecapegfilgrastim, exhibits a favorable safety profile and is effective in preventing severe neutropenia in newly diagnosed DLBCL patients undergoing R‐CHOP or R‐CHOP‐like regimens. Moreover, prophylactic use of mecapegfilgrastim significantly reduces the need for rescue interventions.
